With the same hands that were just poking at sand in the playground, your child grabs a snack and pops it in their mouth. Somehow "go wash your hands" gets brushed off as if unheard.

For a child who finds handwashing a bother and just wants to play, a story works far better than nagging. When you paint invisible germs in a way your child can picture, you can get them heading to the sink on their own.

content.alt: 03. Bubble Bubble, Squeaky Clean! - Why the handwashing habit matters
content.text:
Why the handwashing habit matters

The toddler years are a time of exploring the world with the hands, so building the habit of washing before meals and after outdoor play is a basic of good health. Invisible germs stuck on the hands can ride into the tummy on food and cause a stomachache.

What matters isn't scaring them, but getting the method into their body. Wet them nice and damp, work up a bubbly lather, rinse every corner squeaky clean. Repeat these three steps like a game and your child will start doing it all by themselves.

content.alt: 03. Bubble Bubble, Squeaky Clean! - Kong's tummy ache and handwashing story
content.text:
Kong's tummy ache and handwashing story

Kong, from Bubble Bubble, Squeaky Clean!, eats bread with sandy hands and then his tummy goes rumble, aching softly inside. As tears well up in Kong's eyes, his friend Hori rushes right over.

The two stand side by side at the sink and do it together: one, wet them damp; two, work up a bubbly lather; three, rinse every corner squeaky clean. The little germ wrigglers clinging to their fingertips wash right down the drain, and Kong's hands are soft and sparkling!

content.alt: 03. Bubble Bubble, Squeaky Clean! - Putting handwashing into practice at home
content.text:
Putting handwashing into practice at home

Once you've read the story, it's time to carry it into practice at home. Here are a few ideas.

First, read this book together before meals and after outdoor play. The afterglow of the story flows straight into handwashing. Second, do the three steps of wet, lather, and rinse together while counting one, two, three. Third, rub the easy-to-miss spots like the backs of the hands and between the fingers, and praise loudly those soft, clean hands when they're all done.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How should I teach my child to wash their hands?

A. Show them the process of working up bubbles and rubbing between the fingers like a game. When you talk about why we wash hands using a toddler handwashing habit storybook, their wish to do it themselves grows.

Q. How long should they wash their hands?

A. Long enough to sing a short song is plenty for a fun, thorough wash. Rather than timing it, enjoy the process of building up plenty of bubbles and rinsing squeaky clean together.

Q. How do I teach them when to wash their hands?

A. Set fixed moments and repeat them, like when coming home, before meals, and after using the toilet, and your child will remember on their own. Big praise for washing well makes the habit solid.
